content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"The harlot symbolizes covenant unfaithfulness to God — idolatry, apostasy, and illicit alliances by a people bound to God (Hosea 1–3; Ezek 16, 23; Jer 2–3). In Revelation 17–18 the 'great harlot Babylon' is a seductive anti-God system; the referent is debated, with imperial Rome dominant, apostate church and world-system common, and Jerusalem an acknowledged minority (preterist) alternative.","book_summary":"The harlot is the covenant-breaker who keeps the outward form of covenant without its substance — 'that great city,' spiritually Sodom, Egypt, Babylon: unfaithful Jerusalem. The book explicitly rejects the common identification of Revelation's harlot with Rome, identifying her instead with Jerusalem via the 'great city' linkage of Rev 17:18 and Rev 11:8.","consensus_core_identification":"Symbol of spiritual/covenantal adultery by a people covenanted to God; in Revelation, a corrupt seductive system called Babylon, whose historical referent is contested (Rome dominant, Jerusalem a minority option).","book_core_identification":"Covenant unfaithfulness embodied specifically in Jerusalem — the covenant people wearing covenant form without substance — identified as Revelation's 'great city' harlot, explicitly not Rome.","core_relation":"BOOK_NARROWS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book preserves the consensus's central category (covenant infidelity by a covenanted party) but narrows the referent field: it fixes Revelation's harlot as Jerusalem, excluding Rome, the apostate institutional church, and the generic world-system readings that the consensus treats as dominant or common. Cases the consensus admits (Rome's imperial cult and commerce, papal/apostate Christendom, transhistorical Babylon) are reclassified out; the OT Jerusalem-as-harlot cases (Isa 1:21; Ezek 16, 23) are retained and made central.","material_contradiction":"The book contradicts the commonly taught referent of Revelation 17–18 ('Rome, not Jerusalem' is what it flags as the common view it rejects), but this contradicts the consensus's dominant alternative for one passage's referent, not the consensus's core symbolic identification, which the consensus itself describes as unsettled at the referent level and which lists Jerusalem as an established minority (preterist) reading.","rationale":"Both readings agree at the minimum core: harlotry = covenant unfaithfulness/spiritual adultery by a party in covenant with God. The genuine disagreement is over the extension in Revelation 17–18. The consensus lists the book's Jerusalem identification explicitly as a minority alternative (Response A alternative 3, Response B alternative 3, Response C alternative 3), so the book is not NOVEL. Because the central symbolic referent-category is intact and the book's move is a boundary decision within an admittedly unsettled referent debate — adopting a listed minority reading while rejecting the dominant one — REFINED (with material reclassification of the Revelation cases) fits better than DIVERGENT, which would require replacement of the consensus's core identification itself.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue DIVERGENT: the book explicitly denies the identity most consensus interpreters assign to Revelation's harlot (Rome/world-system) and replaces it with Jerusalem, and 'Rome vs. Jerusalem' is a material contradiction about the same referent in the same context. If the referent of Revelation 17–18 is treated as the core identification rather than the abstract symbolic sense, the book replaces the dominant consensus referent rather than merely narrowing it. This is mitigated by the consensus's own statement that the Revelation referent has no settled consensus and by its explicit listing of the Jerusalem reading.","confidence":"medium"}
